source.title: Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning - The Limit of the Scaling Law
source.authors: Tian-Si Dong; M. Jamnik; Pietro Lio

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adding training data can bring data-driven systems to symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning, and argues that data scaling alone cannot ensure that outcome. It does not measure the loss-scaling or compute-allocation versions listed here.
record.gate_note: The experiments measure syllogism accuracy and failures on unintended inputs, not held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling curves, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocations. The retained rows document the paper's relevant data-expansion results; they are linked to no listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper invokes the scaling law (citing Kaplan et al.) as motivation and titles its experiments 'limits of scaling laws'. It measures no loss, fits no power law, and varies no parameters, tokens or compute in a controlled sweep. Its results are syllogism accuracy for a small CNN (Euler Net) across 19 self-learning data-expansion loops, plus GPT-5 accuracy across surface forms. Its argument, that more data cannot reach perfect symbolic-level reasoning, targets a claim none of V1–V7 makes. The data-expansion accuracy gain is not fitted against data size and is not tied to scale or pretraining loss, so it does not test V6 either. The reader's 'tests/T5' label is not warranted.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that two methodological limitations (combination-table training data and conflicting end-to-end targets) mean more data and training time cannot ensure symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning. The paraphrase could add that they frame this as a limit of the scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates syllogistic reasoning in GPT-5 models and Euler Net, including self-learning data expansion; it does not fit or test the original scaling-law loss curves or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports effects associated with input modality and representation, surface lexical pattern, and whether evaluation uses randomly generated inputs, WordNet-derived tasks, or unintended inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-learning data expansion raised Euler Net accuracy on random syllogism inputs from 56.0% to a 97.8% peak at iteration 19, short of 100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding task-specific training data improves logical-reasoning accuracy, but the gains need not reach perfect (symbolic-level) performance.

fits_no_version.finding: After the 19 self-learning loops, Euler Net was 100% accurate on 8 valid types but 76% overall on WordNet-derived tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from added data do not transfer uniformly to evaluation sets that distinguish task subtypes.

fits_no_version.finding: Euler Net misreads novel semicircle inputs even after being trained to 100% accuracy on single-circle unintended inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perfect accuracy on enumerated inputs does not imply robust reasoning on unenumerated inputs.

record.problems: The experiments assess syllogistic accuracy rather than held-out language-model loss or scaling-law fits, so they do not establish whether the specified loss laws hold. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant results.
record.rows_left_out: Not stated: only the relevant data-expansion and unintended-input results are included. The GPT-5 surface-form evaluation and background results attributed to cited studies do not measure any listed scaling-law version.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small-run fits.
All: no shape variation at fixed parameter count.
All: no power-law fit in any modality or regime.
All: downstream accuracy is not related to model scale or pretraining loss. Data-loop accuracy gains are not fitted.
All: no fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling law' in the title is rhetorical. There is no loss, no model-size sweep, and no power-law fit. The GPT-5 surface-form results (Table 1) are correctly left out, since they do not vary scale. The PaLM 2-Small versus PaLM 2-Large comparison is a result cited from [21], not this study's own result. No uncertainty estimates are given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits on small runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their trends with compute.
Effects of architecture depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictable downstream-task performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power-law curves.

rows.subject: Euler Net
rows.operation_detail: Repeated self-learning iterations added newly generated error examples to training data; accuracy was measured on randomly generated test data.
rows.note: The authors report a 2.2% gap from 100%; this is accuracy on the stated task, not pretraining loss or a power-law fit.
rows.check: Accuracy across self-learning iterations on a syllogism task, not loss versus scale. No power-law fit, so the row bears on no version. The authors' line 'supports the law of scaling' is a loose remark, not a fit.

rows.subject: Euler Net with 19 loops of self-learning
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated on a newly created linguistic-input dataset intended to distinguish valid syllogism types.

conditions.value: 14,000 syllogism reasoning tasks derived from WordNet-3.0

rows.value: 76% overall; 100% accuracy on 8 valid types, with accuracies of 50% to 83.3% on the remaining types
rows.note: Aggregate result across the dataset; the paper reports the per-type range and count of types at 100%, not separate values for every type.
rows.check: Single-model evaluation with no scale variation. The paper says 'remaining 16 types' after grouping 24 types into 14 groups, an internal inconsistency the row should note.

rows.subject: Euler Net
rows.operation_detail: Tested on newly introduced unintended inputs formed from colored circles and semicircles after training to classify single-circle inputs as unintended.

conditions.value: green circle and red semicircle in one image; blue semicircle and green circle in the other

rows.measure: qualitative output behavior on unintended inputs
rows.value: Sometimes completed the semicircles into whole circles and predicted the blue circle contains the red circle; the authors state that new unintended patterns remain possible.
rows.note: The text also describes confidence values in Figure 11, but the relevant outputs are presented as figure examples rather than a systematic quantitative result.
rows.check: Qualitative behaviour on unintended inputs. It bears on no scaling-law version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
